transcript:
Meeting header: Aurelia Health — quick sandbox onramp: chatgen params & retry primers
Date: 2025-11-25 15:00 PST | Duration: 47 mins
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Samir Kapoor (Aurelia Eng Lead); Lena Ortiz (Product); Diego Ruiz (SRE)

Auto-summary: quick demo + hands-on kickstart, prioritized reliability and predictable latency for patient-facing chat features.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE, and with me is Priya our systems engineer. How are you folks doing?
[00:06] Samir: Good thanks Jordan, excited — we had a couple PLs lined up, mainly latency constraints for mobile and also a retry story cause we saw some flakiness on our current endpoint.
[00:15] Priya: Great, we'll walk through a sandbox live, show streaming behavior, parameter knobs and recommended retry patterns. Also quick Console tour for Optimize suggestions.
[00:25] Lena: Appreciate that, our PM goals: keep median latency under 250ms for short prompts, and keep cost within budget. We also need a secure path for PHI — Diego will speak to that.
[00:38] Diego: Yep SOC2 and VPC are table stakes. We want to know what data is persisted and how to rotate keys.
[00:44] Jordan: Totally. Quick agenda: 1) live sandbox streaming demo 2) parameter tuning 3) retry/playback strategies 4) Console optimize + security notes 5) next steps. Sound good?
[00:53] Samir: Yep.

--- Live sandbox demo ---
[01:20] Priya: I'm going to share my screen, launching a quick chatgen call via the hosted API. Note — we're streaming tokens back as chunked responses, so you see partial output as it's generated.
[01:35] Priya: (typing) POST /v1/chat/completions -> model: redwood-chat-1, stream: true, messages: [...]. Temperature 0.2, max_tokens 120.
[01:51] Samir: When you set stream true, what's the exact behavior on reconnects if the client drops? Do we get idempotent resumes?
[02:00] Priya: Short answer: no automatic resume for partial streams. We recommend using idempotency keys at request granularity so you can safely retry the whole request. For interactive clients we also show token checkpoints in the response metadata so you can detect duplication.
[02:20] Jordan: Also, we often suggest a short client-side buffer and reconnect strategy: if the socket drops, attempt a single quick reconnect with the same idempotency token and, on server side, we dedupe completed requests.
[02:33] Diego: So server dedupe is based on idempotency token + model + input hash?
[02:38] Priya: Exactly — we hash the prompt+metadata and pair with the idempotency token to avoid accidental double-charges. If the original request completed, the server returns the same response reference.
[02:49] Lena: Nice. How do stop tokens behave in streaming mode — like partial flushes?
[02:55] Priya: Stop tokens are applied at generation time; streaming frames stop once a stop condition is emitted. However, if you have very short timeouts you might see the last chunk repeated in a reconnect, so again idempotency plus client-side dedupe helps.

[03:20] Priya: I'll demonstrate parameter effects — first low temp 0.0, deterministic short response. (runs) You can see responses are crisp but maybe terse.
[03:40] Priya: Now bump temp to 0.9 and top_p 0.9 for more creative outputs. That increases token variance and slightly increases tail latency per token for some models.
[04:00] Samir: Is it common to use top_p and temperature together? Any heuristic?
[04:06] Priya: Yes — temperature controls randomness in logits scaling, top_p does nucleus sampling. We recommend either tuning temp first (0.0–0.4 for deterministic), or using top_p around 0.8 for a controlled diversity. Console Optimize can profile your prompt corpus and suggest a sweet spot per workload.

--- Retry strategy deep-dive ---
[05:10] Jordan: Ok now retries — common tradeoff: naive retry increases cost and duplicates user-visible content. We propose: idempotency tokens for any non-idempotent write; exponential backoff with jitter; and client-side dedupe for display.
[05:30] Samir: What about partial success where some tokens were emitted but we didn't get full completion ack?
[05:36] Priya: Two patterns: 1) treat stream as best-effort — on reconnect, present the room for continued generation from server if you keep track of last confirmed token index; 2) easier for most apps: re-request with same idempotency token — server returns completed response if available, else regenerates and returns final sequence. Our SDKs have helpers for idempotency management.
[06:00] Diego: Any guidance for retry counts and backoff windows?
[06:05] Priya: Default we recommend 3 attempts with base delay 200ms and exponential factor x2 with jitter capped at ~2s for interactive workflows. For batch jobs you can be more patient. Also watch error classes — 429s (rate limit) vs 5xx (transient infra) vs 4xx (client). Different handling per class.
[06:26] Lena: If we implement client side streaming and a user sees duplicate sentences after a reconnect, is that covered by the idempotency approach?
[06:34] Priya: Partially. Idempotency prevents double billing and avoids generating multiple final outputs server-side. For UI dedupe you'll need to detect repeated prefixes. We suggest prefix hash + server-provided token offset in the stream frames.

[07:10] Priya: Quick Console demo — Optimize tab shows per-route suggestions: batching windows, cache TTL suggestions, and quantization recommendations if on Dedicated/Private. For hosted, we show inferred batch sizes and expected cost savings if you enable prefix caching.
[07:33] Jordan: For Aurelia, short clinical prompts should see high benefit from KV/prefix caching if many prompts share context (patient template). Optimize would suggest cache TTL and when to enable it.
[07:45] Samir: Is caching safe for PHI?
[07:48] Diego: that's our worry.
[07:50] Priya: Good callout. We never persist sensitive data unless customer opts in — for hosted customers with PHI needs we discuss Private/VPC offers. Even with caching, you can configure encryption-at-rest and KMS integration, and set TTL to zero to avoid persistence. We'll include the security doc link.

--- Questions & security ---
[09:05] Lena: Can you summarize data flow for hosted mode? Where do logs go?
[09:11] Jordan: Short: request hits Redwood API, routed to a runtime pod; logs and traces are stored in the control plane with audit logging; for hosted customers we retain minimal metadata and you can opt into longer retention via enterprise agreement. All of that is in the SOC2 packet we will share.
[09:26] Diego: KMS rotation — do you support customer-managed keys?
[09:30] Priya: Yes, we support KMS/HSM integrations for Dedicated and Private. For hosted we offer managed keys but can integrate customer KMS for enterprise plans.

[10:00] Samir: Back to streaming — any caveats on mobile clients with flaky networks? Do you recommend polling instead?
[10:08] Priya: For very flaky networks we sometimes recommend turning streaming off and using synchronous responses with smaller max_tokens, or implementing a hybrid: start with stream and fall back to polling on repeated disconnects. Streaming is better UX if connections are stable, but mobile edge conditions vary.

[12:30] Jordan: Let's talk about costs quickly — token usage depends on prompt + completion. We recommend using shorter system prompts, and the Console shows per-token cost breakdown. Optimize can propose lowering max_tokens or using a cheaper model for background tasks.
[12:48] Lena: Could we route lower-sensitivity tasks to a cheaper model automatically?
[12:52] Priya: Yes — Smart routing rules let you send requests to cheaper model variants by route/intent, and we automatically fallback to higher-tier models for safety-critical routes.

[14:00] Priya: Demo: show retry example — I’ll force a temporary 5xx on the runtime to show client backoff and idempotency behavior. (fires) You can see the SDK logs show a single re-request with same idempotency token and the server returning final output; no duplicate charges.
[14:28] Samir: Ok that helps.

[15:00] Jordan: Quick note on observability — Console has per-request traces, latency percentiles, token counts, and per-token cost. You can export traces to your pager or SIEM.
[15:12] Diego: Can we integrate with Datadog?
[15:15] Priya: Yes, we have export hooks and can send traces/events — we'll include a sample integration link in the follow-up.

[16:00] Jordan: Time check — we have about 30 mins left. Any high-priority areas?
[16:06] Samir: We'd like a short pilot with our typical traffic shape and a focus on median latency and retry behavior. Also need security packet.
[16:12] Jordan: Sounds good — we'll prep the sandbox and pilot plan.

--- deeper technical seed questions ---
[17:05] Diego: On KV cache — does it cache per model session or global per-customer? How do you handle eviction?
[17:12] Priya: KV cache is per-customer by default, configurable per-route. Eviction is LRU with TTL, and the Console can show hit/miss rates. For very sensitive data you can disable caching for particular routes.
[17:26] Samir: For patient-facing autocomplete we worry about hallucination if cache returns stale context. Any guidance?
[17:32] Priya: We recommend conservative TTLs and active invalidation via API when patient context changes. Optimize can flag stale-hit rates and suggest TTL adjustments.

[19:00] Priya: Quick note on model quantization — on Dedicated we can run quantized variants to reduce inference latency and cost; Console Optimize shows expected perf delta and quality tradeoff.
[19:20] Lena: If we move to Dedicated for compliance, what's the expected timeline?
[19:24] Jordan: Typically 4–8 weeks for capacity reservation and private networking, depending on region and approval cycles.

[20:00] Samir: For the pilot, what sample size should we use to get meaningful latency numbers?
[20:05] Priya: For median latency a few hundred short requests (100–500) across peak/off-peak is usually enough. For P99 you'd want larger samples. We'll help design the harness.

[21:40] Jordan: Alright wrapping up, quick recap: we'll send pricing, SOC2 & VPC docs, provision sandbox, and schedule a 2-hour hands-on with Priya. Aurelia to share traffic pattern and SLOs. Pilot target: capture median latency & cost baseline over 48h.
[21:58] Lena: That works.
[22:05] Samir: Thanks both.
[22:08] Diego: Appreciate it.
[22:12] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links and next steps.

End meeting.
